newsitem.title: FINLAND: Helsinki summit hosts embrace non-aligned role.
newsitem.headline: Helsinki summit hosts embrace non-aligned role.

text.p: A local newspaper cartoon this week neatly parodied non-aligned Finland's security options: when it comes to membership of the NATO military alliance, it said, Finland can say "no" either in Finnish or Russian.

Hosts to this week's U.S.-Russian summit and in a unique position as a European Union member on the border with Russia, Finland insists on its independence as it debates its role in the European landscape.

Questions have been surfacing about whether formerly neutral Finland, which joined the EU in 1995, should follow former Soviet bloc states and seek to join the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation. The government's answer remains a steadfast "no".

But in an echo of suspicion fuelled by the relative secrecy of Finland's Cold War years with a Soviet friendship pact, polls show a majority of Finns oppose NATO membership, yet nearly all believe the government is preparing to join.
In the week Presidents Bill Clinton and Boris Yeltsin were due to hold their summit, parliamentarians reaffirmed Finland's non-aligned future in a three-day debate on defence.

Yeltsin caused a stir at the start of the week when he used an interview with the leading daily Helsingin Sanomat to compliment Finland on its decision to remain non-aligned -- a message seen as telling Finland it must stay out of NATO.

But the Finns, who fought two wars against the former Soviet Union and trod a delicate East-West line in the Cold War, insist their non-alignment boosts Europe's security and quietly believe they can help some other countries handle Russia.

"We really do believe our best position is to stay out," said one diplomat. "We don't want to rock a boat which already looks pretty unstable. In the future too, Russia's neighbours will have a special place and need a special way of thinking."

Instead of the highly visible political statement made by joining NATO, they are building links with the West through lower profile channels including NATO's Partnership for Peace programme and other diplomatic forums.

The Finns believe this approach can help the Baltic states, Finland's southern neighbours and strategically key both for Russia and the Nordic countries, which are widely expected to be excluded from the first round of NATO expansion.

"We are approaching NATO's enlargement issue as a country which, having stabilised its position, sort of produces security for its environment and for the whole of Europe," said Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen earlier this week.

Finland and Sweden said on Tuesday they would intensify cooperation with Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania -- teaching local languages to their Russian-speaking populations and helping them organise border controls. Sweden is neutral and an EU member.
Although minor projects, the timing of the announcement is a clear and deliberate gesture as Russia sticks to its tough line against NATO expansion, diplomats said.

"I think we will see much more of this toughening from Russia in coming years. This is normal behaviour for Russians," said one. "In the years since the collapse of communism we are facing the fact that it did not produce an Eden.
"Our role is to take a calm, serious and pragmatic approach. In that, we may be able to help our neighbours."
